abstract: Summary Influenza A virus (IAV) infection remodels cellular processes to support viral replication. The modulation of host factors by the virus drives pathogenesis during infection, and these factors may serve as therapeutic targets. Here, we infect mice with two IAV strains, H1N1 and H5N1, and analyze lung tissue with multi-omics. Using network propagation analysis, we identify twenty-four distinct host modules altered by infection, encompassing 2920 genes/proteins. Independently, we develop a computational pipeline, MidTOD, which integrates metabolomic data with other OMICs data-types, linking metabolites to gene/protein alterations. Combining datasets from both approaches reveals alterations in mitochondrial and peroxisomal metabolism in IAV-infected cells and identifies arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (GATM) as a host dependency factor in both human cells and mice. Knockdown of this enzyme reduces IAV-mediated pathology and host inflammatory responses after infection. Collectively, this work provides an integrated systems-level view of host changes during infection and identifies an abundance of IAV-host factors.

Experimental models and study participant details
Mice
Female C57BL/6 mice, aged six to eight weeks, were purchased from Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME) and used for the OMICs profiling. Six week old female BALB/cJ mice were used for PPMO experiments.
Cell culture models
Human tracheobronchial epithelial (HTBE) cells (Lonza, Donor 4F1289J) were cultured at 37°C and 5% CO2 in commercially available airway epithelial cell basal medium following ATCC protocol. These cells were derived from one donor and all tissues used for isolation of these cells were obtained under informed consent and conform to HIPAA standards to protect the privacy of the donors’ personal health information. A549 (ATCC CCL-185) cells were cultured in T175 flasks (Fisher, 12-556-011) at 37°C and 5% CO2 in DMEM with L-glutamine without sodium pyruvate (Fisher, MT 10-017-CV), 10% FBS (Life Technologies, A3160502) and 1X Penicillin/Streptomycin (P/S, Fisher, MT 30-002-CI).
Method details
Infections
California/4/09 (H1N1); Vietnam/1203/04 (H5N1-HALo) strains of IAV were generated at Mt. Sinai School of Medicine. Six to eight week-old female C57BL/6 mice (Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME) were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of a mixture of ketamine and xylazine (100 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg, respectively), and then 50 μL of infectious virus diluted in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) was inoculated intranasally (i.n.). To determine virus pathogenicity, five animals per group were infected i.n. with dose (1 × 10
4
PFU) and were monitored daily for weight loss for up to 14 days post infection (p.i.). Mice showing more than 25% of body weight loss were considered to have reached predefined humane endpoints and were euthanized. To determine viral pulmonary replication kinetics and to examine for genomics, proteomics and metabolomics, groups of 15 mice were inoculated with the indicated viruses (1 × 10
4
PFU per mouse). Mice inoculated with PBS served as controls. At 12h, 1, 2, 3 and 4 days p.i., 3 mice per experimental group were euthanized. Control animals were euthanized at 12h and 4 days post inoculation. The control animals sacrificed at 12h served as a control for IAV-infected animals at 12h, 1, and 2 days p.i. and the control animals sacrificed at 4 days p.i. served as the control for IAV-infected animals at day 3 and 4, respectively. For determination of viral titers, lungs were homogenized in 1 mL of PBS and viral titers determined by plaque assays with MDCK cells. To examine genomics, proteomics and metabolomics, lungs were homogenized in liquid nitrogen and divided in three equal amounts; also, homogenized lung samples were weighted, recorded, and shipped for analysis to genomics, proteomics and metabolomics cores. All animal studies were performed according to institutional guidelines and approved by the institutional care and use committee at Mt. Sinai School of Medicine.
Transcriptomics
To begin RNA extraction, mouse lungs were homogenized in liquid nitrogen. 1 mL Trizol was added per 50–100 mg of tissue and the homogenate was incubated at room temperature for 5 min 200 μL chloroform were added per mL of Trizol, shaken vigorously for 15–30 s and incubated at room temperature for 15 min. Samples were centrifuged for 15 min at 4°C and 12,000 rcf. The aqueous phase was carefully collected in a separate tube. 500 μL isopropanol was added per 1 mL Trizol, inverted to mix and incubated at room temperature for 5–10 min. Samples were transferred to Qiagen RNeasy Spin Columns and RNA was isolated according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA-seq libraries were constructed using the Illumina TruSeq Stranded Total RNA Library Prep Kit and samples were sequenced with an Illumina HiSeq 2500.
Sequencing reads were aligned to the California/4/09 (H1N1), Vietnam/1203/04 (H5N1-HALo), or mouse mm10 genome assembly using STAR,
92
which also produced segment- or gene-wise read counts. Differential gene expression analysis was carried out using DESeq2,
93
producing maximum likelihood log2 fold change (FC) values and Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted
p
-values via the Wald test. Heatmaps were drawn using non-blinded regularized log values from DESeq2.
Preparation of samples for global ubiquitination, phosphorylation, and protein abundance analysis
Frozen mouse lung tissue was homogenized in liquid nitrogen to a powder, resuspended in 8 M urea, 50 mM NH
4
HCO
3
, 150 mM NaCl, and PhosStop and Complete-EDTA free phosphatase and protease inhibitors (Roche), sonicated 3 times for 1 s at 30% power, and debris pelleted by centrifugation. Lysates were reduced by the addition of 4 mM TCEP (Sigma) for 30 min at room temperature, disulfide bonds were alkylated with 10 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma) for 30 min in the dark at room temperature, and excess iodoacetamide was quenched with 20 mM DTT (Sigma). Lysates were diluted 1:4 in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and trypsin (Promega) was added at a 1:100 enzyme:substrate ratio. Lysates were digested for 18 h at room temperature with rotation. Digested lysates were acidified to 0.1% TFA and peptides concentrated on Sep-Pak C18 solid phase extraction columns (Waters).
For protein abundance analysis, an amount of digested lysate equivalent to 100 μg of protein from each sample was labeled with TMT6-plex reagent according to the manufacturer’s instructions then combined. The following TMT reagents were used for all samples of each time point: 12h: TMT127, 24h: TMT128, 48h: TMT129, 72h: TMT130, 96h: TMT131, mock: TMT126. TMT-labeled peptides were fractionated by hydrophilic interaction chromatography (HILIC). Peptides were injected onto a TKSgel amide-80 column (Tosoh biosciences, 2.0 mm × 15 cm packed with 5 μm particles), equilibrated with 10% HILIC Buffer A (2% ACN, 0.1% TFA) and 90% HILIC Buffer B (98% ACN, 0.1% TFA) using an AKTA P10 purifier system. The samples were then separated by a 1-h gradient from 90% HILIC Buffer B to 55% HILIC Buffer B at a flow rate of 0.3 mL/min. Fractions were collected every 1.5 min and combined into 8 fractions based on the 280 nm absorbance chromatogram. Fractions were evaporated to dryness and reconstituted in 20 μL of 0.1% formic acid for mass spectrometry analysis.
For ubiquitin remnant analysis, an amount of digested lysate equivalent to 10 mg of protein was subjected to ubiquitin remnant immunoprecipitation according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Cell Signaling Technologies). For phosphorylation analysis, an amount of digested lysate equivalent to 1 mg of protein was lyophilized and then resuspended in a buffer containing 75% ACN with 0.1% TFA. Peptides were incubated with Fe
3+
-immobilized metal affinity chromatography (IMAC), washed with the same resuspension buffer, and then phosphopeptides were eluted with 500 mM HK
2
PO
4
. For both ubiquitin remnant-enriched and phosphopeptide-enriched samples, the purified material was desalted using homemade C18 STAGE tips, evaporated to dryness, and then resuspended in 0.1% formic acid for mass spectrometry analysis.
94
Proteomics acquisition
All digested, desalted and dried peptides were resuspended in 4% formic acid, 3% acetonitrile. 2 μL of each sample were injected in technical singlet by an Easy-nLC 1000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) interfaced via a nanoelectrospray source (Nanospray Flex) coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) or an Orbitrap Elite mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher scientific) operating in positive ion mode. Injected peptides were separated on a C18 reverse phase column (75 μm × 25 cm packed with 1.9 μm Reprosil-Pur C18 AQ reversed-phase resin) over the course of a 120 min data acquisition (abundance and ubiquitylation) or 240 min data acquisition (phosphorylation). Buffer A consisted of 0.1% formic acid (FA) in water, and buffer B was 0.1% FA in acetonitrile.
For H1N1 protein abundance samples, data was collected on the Orbitrap Elite mass spectrometer, with spectra being continuously acquired in a data-dependent manner using a TMT-SPS method.
95
Specifically, one full scan in the Orbitrap (at 60,000 resolution in profile mode with an AGC target of 1×10
5
) was followed by 10 MS/MS scans events in the linear ion trap. Monoisotopic precursor selection was enabled, unassigned and +1 charge states were rejected, and dynamic exclusion with a repeat count of 1 within 20s was enabled. For MS/MS events an intensity threshold of 500, CID collision energy of 35%, 2 m/z isolation width was used. From each MS/MS event, the most abundant ion was selected for MS
3
to acquire TMT reporter ion intensities. The MS
3
events had a minimum intensity threshold of 500, 4 m/z isolation width, HCD fragmentation at 60% normalized collision energy with a 100 m/z first fixed mass.
For H5N1 protein abundance samples, spectra were continuously acquired in a data-dependent manner using a TMT-SPS method. Specifically, one full scan in the Orbitrap (at 120,000 resolution in profile mode with an AGC target of 5×10
5
and maximum injection time of 150 ms) was followed by as many MS/MS scans as could be acquired on the most abundant ions in 3 s in the dual linear ion trap (rapid scan type with an intensity threshold of 500, HCD collision energy of 35%, AGC target of 1 × 30
4
, maximum injection time of 150 ms, and isolation width of 1.6 m/z). Charge states 2–7 were selected for this. Dynamic exclusion was enabled with a repeat count of 1, an exclusion duration of 30 s, and an exclusion mass width of ±10 ppm. From these MS/MS scans, the 5 most abundant fragment ions were selected for MS
3
to obtain reporter ion quantification. For this, selected ions were fragmented by HCD (27% collision energy) with a first mass set to 100 m/z and detection in the orbitrap at 15,000 resolution in centroid mode with a maximum injection time of 250 ms and an AGC target of 1 × 10
5
.
For all protein phosphorylation and ubiquitylation samples, MS1 spectra were collected in the Orbitrap in profile mode from 200 to 2000
m/z
with a 1e6 AGC target and 100 ms maximum injection time. The top 20 most abundant ions were selected for MS2, with filtering criteria for selection being a minimum signal of 500, a defined charge state of z > 1. Furthermore, dynamic exclusion with a repeat count of 1, a duration of 20 s, and an exclusion width of 10 ppm was enabled. Selected precursors were isolated with a 2 m/z isolation width, and fragmented with resonance-excitation collision-induced dissociation using a normalized collision energy of 35%, an activation Q of 0.25, and a 10 ms activation time, a 1e4 AGC target, and a 10 ms maximum injection time.
Proteomics data processing
Raw MS files from IAV infection time course samples were grouped separately by enrichment (abundance vs. phosphorylation vs. ubiquitylation), and instrument, and searched simultaneously within each group using MaxQuant (version 1.6.3.3).
96
MS/MS spectra were searched against the mouse proteome (SwissProt human canonical sequences, downloaded 04 September 2018) and IAV protein sequences. Trypsin (KR|P) was selected to allow up to two missed cleavages. Variable modifications were assigned for: N-terminal protein acetylation, and methionine oxidation. One static modification was assigned for carbamidomethyl cysteine. LFQ was enabled. Match between runs disabled. All other MaxQuant settings were left at the default.
The R packages MSstatsTMT and MSstats were used for quantitative analysis of abundance and PTM proteomics, respectively. Protein abundance was summarized from peptide abundance with the function proteinSummarization with defaults except peptide normalization was turned off, and summarization was by method “logSum” which uses a log transformed sum of peptide abundance. For PTM, both phosphorylation (PH) and ubiquitylation (UB), the peptide ion intensities were summarized to a single intensity per unique observed single-peptide combination of modified sites (either PH or UB) by relabeling the protein of each feature as the combination of protein name and observed modified sites. The Bioconductor package artMS (version 1.3.9) (
https://doi.org/10.18129/B9.bioc.artMS
) was used for this relabeling, and the dataProcess function of MSstats was used for summarization with default parameters. The differences in log2-transformed intensity between infected and mock samples were scored using the MSstats function groupComparison or MSstatsTMT function groupComparisonTMT, which fit a single linear model for each protein with a single categorical variable for condition. From these models, these functions report pairwise differences in means between conditions as log2FC with a
p
-value based on a two-sided t-test assuming equal variance across all conditions, and report adjusted
p
-values using the false discovery rate (FDR) estimated by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.
Network propagation analysis
Network propagation was performed for all datasets—transcriptomics, abundance proteomics (AB), phosphoproteomics (PH) and ubiquitination proteomics (UB)—separately on the background of a STRING network using all edges with a score >600 (60% confidence). This STRING network comprises 18,966 genes connected by 976,668 edges. The maximum -log10(
p
) value per gene across time points and, in the case of UB and PH data, all sites, was used as starting “heat” to propagate. Propagation per omics type without mixing of different types of starting heat was performed by random walk with restart, with a restart probability of 0.2. The final score significance of propagated heat was determined by permutation analysis, permuting the starting heat among observed-genes-per-omics; 20,000 permutations. For permutation analysis, “self-heat” is subtracted from propagated heat, so that we only consider the heat propagated from other nodes on the network. “Self-heat” is defined as the portion of propagated-heat at each node that is the result of starting heat at that node. Additionally, the same network propagation was performed on the UB and PH datasets adjusted by AB. Finally, filtered RNA-seq data by adj.p.value <0.01 and abs(log2FC) > 2 was combined with the previous datasets, requiring
p
< 0.002 based on permutation analysis for all network propagation scores, resulting in a set of 2,920 significant genes.
Some RNA-seq genes could not be mapped to STRING identifiers, resulting in a set of 2463 genes for subsequent clustering. Clustering was performed using Diffusion State Distance (DSD)
97
to measure gene distances on a further subset of the STRING network that included only edges between the 2463 genes. DSD evaluates inter-gene distance based on similar results of random walks from the two genes, and was a major portion of the best overall method for network module detection in Choobdar et al
.
98
The DSD distance matrix was clustered using the partition around medoids procedure implemented in the
pam
function in the
cluster
package of R. Setting k to 24 modules (clusters) was chosen based on a local maximum in clustering score (average silhouette width), as measured by the
pamk
function in the
fpc
package, and visual inspection of the clustered distance matrix (see
Figure S2
).
Kinase activity
Relative kinase activity scores were calculated using known kinase-substrate relationships in literature.
34
The resource is a comprehensive collection of kinase-substrate relationships obtained from six databases, PhosphoSitePlus, SIGNOR, HPRD, NCI-PID, Reactome, and the BEL Large Corpus, and using three text-mining tools, REACH, Sparser, and RLIMS-P. Relative kinase activities were scored with a Z-test from the comparison of fold changes in phosphosite measurements of the known substrates against the overall distribution of fold changes across the sample. This statistical approach has been previously shown to perform well at estimating kinase activities.
33
,
99
P-values across kinases were adjusted for multiple testing by controlling the false discovery rate using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure in the R function p.adjust.
Cell type fraction estimation (alternatively digital cytometry)
CIBERSORTx
37
,
38
was used to estimate cell type frequencies from RNA-seq gene expression profiles with the droplet-based single-cell lung dataset from Tabula Muris
39
serving as a reference. To build the single-cell reference matrix, up to 150 cells from each cell type were randomly sampled without replacement, yielding 1,599 cells in total. Within the CIBERSORTx environment, the reference matrix was processed to generate a custom signature matrix using default parameters. CIBERSORTx was then used to impute cell fractions from our RNA-seq expression profiles with quantile normalization disabled. The statistical significance of differences across strains and time points was evaluated using a two-way ANOVA, with
p
-values adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing using the Bonferroni method.
Metabolomics
Polar and nonpolar metabolites were extracted from lung sample sets using a modified protocol developed by Bligh and Dyer.
100
Briefly, tissue was harvested in 100 μL methanol and lysed by three rounds of vortex (30 s), sonication, and snap freezing in liquid nitrogen (1 min/thaw). Polar and nonpolar metabolites were separated by partitioning after the addition of 750 μL 2:1 methanol:chloroform, 250 μL chloroform, and 250 μL water followed by vortex. Samples were stored at −20°C for 1 h and then centrifuged for 10 min at 10K rcf. The organic and aqueous phases were separated, and vacuum concentrated to dryness. Dried samples were stored at −80°C until analysis. Aqueous phase samples were reconstituted in 50 μL of 35% (v/v) acetonitrile in water and 5 μL of the sample was injected into the instrument for analysis. Polar metabolites were separated on a Micro200 LC (Eksigent) by hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC; Luna 3um NH2, 150 × 1 mm, 100 Å, Phenomenex). Mobile phase A consisted of water and 5 mM ammonium acetate, pH adjusted to 7.4 with ammonium hydroxide. Mobile phase B consisted of acetonitrile with 5 mM ammonium acetate (pH 7.4). The chromatographic method followed a gradient elution at 30 μL/min with the following conditions: 0–0.5 min 98% B, 0.5–1 min 95% B, 1–5 min 80% B, 5–6 min 46% B, 6–13 min 14.7% B, 13–17 min 0% B, 17–17.1 min 100% B, 17–23 min 100% B. The column eluent was directly flowed into a TripleTOF 5600+ mass spectrometer (Sciex, Framingham, MA) and analyzed in positive mode under the following parameters: 15 psi nebulizer gas, 20 psi heater gas, ion spray voltage 5000 eV, declustering potential 100 eV, TOF MS scan 60–1000 Da, fragmentation collision spread 25–40 eV. Data was acquired by Information Dependent Acquisition (IDA).
Metabolomics data processing and MidTOD development
Mass spectrometry data was aligned by retention time on Markerview software (Sciex, v. 1.2.1). Spectral peaks were aligned using the following parameters: 0.01 min minimum retention time, 0.50 min retention time tolerance, 0.05 Da mass tolerance, 0.01 Da minimum spectral peak width, 2 scan minimum retention time peak width, 8000 maximum number of peaks, peaks removed if found in less than 3 samples and area integrated from raw data. The resulting aligned peak lists were subjected to statistical analysis using artMS (Bioconductor), which formats metabolomics input files to be compatible with MSstats, an R-based statistical analysis software originally designed for proteomics data analysis. This pipeline analyzes spectral peaks, or features, identified by m/z and retention time, and evaluates the differences in peak intensities between treated and control samples. Default artMS settings were used, and the results are reported as pairwise differences in means between conditions as log2FC with a
p
value based on a two-sided t-test assuming equal variance across all conditions.
p
values were adjusted using the false discovery rate (FDR) estimated by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. A log2FC range of (±) 1.0 and FDR of 0.05 were selected for cutoff parameters. Metabolites were identified from the filtered peak list by Metabolite Identification Through Orthologous Datasets (MidTOD;
https://github.com/kroganlab/MIDTOD
). This custom R-based software was designed to integrate the metabolomics spectral data with data from related genomics and proteomics experiments. Metabolites are putatively identified by automated searching of the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database and the Human Metabolome Database (
https://hmdb.ca/
)
101
by molecular weight with a mass threshold of (±) 0.05 Da and a maximum molecular weight of 500 Da. Database hits are then restricted to metabolites that are matched to biologically linked proteins and genes found to be dysregulated by flu infection by the genomics and proteomics cores of the FluOMICs project (i.e., transcriptomics and proteomics analysis (see above and
Table S1
)) and eliminates hits that cannot be matched to other datasets. The MidTOD output consists of a list of putative identifications linked to significantly altered genes and proteins that are validated by matching MS/MS patterns and retention times to authentic standards. Common adducts (H+, NH4+, Na+, K+) are accounted for in the mass search.
MidTOD performance was tested using a decoy dataset containing metabolites identified with level 1 confidence to assess the accuracy of identification versus manual searching of the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB). Each m/z value was analyzed in MidTOD in both positive and negative mode for the +H or –H adduct, respectively. Results were matched to decoy dataset inputs to assess 1) if the correct identification was pulled and 2) the total number of putative identifications each feature was matched to. Features from the decoy dataset were input into HMDB mass search under the same parameters as MidTOD (positive and negative mode, H adduct only). HMDB results were assessed by determining if the correct identification was pulled and how many total possible identifications were assigned. Percentage of the correct identifications over the total possible identifications per feature was graphed using Graphpad Prism. Benchmarking was performed by comparing the overlap of metabolite and pathway identifications to Mummichog 3 (
https://mum3-prod.jax.org/#/analysis/new-analysis
)
102
with the following parameters: positive mode +H adduct, error 20 ppm, 0.05 significance cutoff, 100 permutations and MetaboAnalyst 6.0
44
(
https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/
) with the parameters: Mus musculus-kegg, positive mode, +H adduct.
A549 siRNA screen
To test the effect of genes on IAV infection and replication, an siRNA screen was performed in A549 cells using pools of 4 gene-targeting siRNA.
103
In 24-well format, 6 × 10
4
/well A549 cells were reverse transfected with final concentration 75 nM gene-targeting siRNA (Dharmacon, siGENOME siRNA SMARTpool cherry picked pre-designed library), final concentration 75 nM siGENOME non-targeting siRNA pool #2 (Dharmacon, D-001206-14-05) or 30 nM final concentration NP-targeting siRNA (Dharmacon, custom sequence 5′ GGA UCU UAU UUC UUC GGA GUU 3′) using 2 μL/well Lipofectamine RNAiMAX Transfection Reagent (Thermo Fisher, 13778075). Each gene knockdown was performed in duplicate. After 48 h, cells were infected at MOI 0.1 with Influenza strain A/WSN/1933 H1N1 virus. After 24 h post-infection, cells were lifted and fixed in 1% formaldehyde (Sigma, F8775-500 ML) to determine percent infection by immunostaining for IAV nucleoprotein and flow cytometry. Cells were permeabilized in 1% Bovine Serum Albumin (BSA, GoldBio, A-420-100), 0.1% saponin (Sigma, 47036-50G-F) in 1X PBS (Fisher, MT 21-030-CV), and stained with anti-influenza A nucleoprotein (NP) [HT103] antibody (Kerafast, EMS010) at 1:1000 dilution followed by goat anti-mouse IgG (H + L) secondary antibody Alexa Fluor Plus 488 (Fisher, A32723) at 1:1000 dilution. NP staining was quantified in 96-well format by Attune NxT flow cytometer (Thermo Fisher). All data analysis to quantitate virus infection was performed with FlowJo version 9.3.2 software, using a consistent template for gating (
Figure 6
A). Briefly, A549 cell gate was defined based on forward (FSC)/sideward (SSC)-Area axes, followed by two successive singlet gates: FSC-Height versus FSC-Width and SSC-Height versus SSC-Width. Alexa Fluor 488+ cells were defined as NP + cells in this final population, with gates defined in Blue Laser 1-Area versus FSC-Area for FSC-Area above 200,000 and Alexa Fluor 488 signal above 1000. For scoring, wells with ≥50% cells in the A549 gate as defined by FSC/SSC (gating step 1) were excluded from further analysis. Log2 fold-change was calculated relative to the median of all non-targeting siRNAs per plate with values ≥ |2| considered a ‘hit’ (
Table S6
).
HTBE siRNA experiments
To evaluate the effect of GATM knockdown in IAV replication, HTBE cells were transfected with siRNAs targeting GATM (Dharmacon siGENOME M-008900-01) or IAV NP (Dharmacon, custom sequence 5′ GGA UCU UAU UUC UUC GGA GUU 3′), or a negative control non-targeting siRNA (Dharmacon, custom sequence 5′-AAT CGA TCA TAG GAC GAA CGC-3′). Transfections were carried out in 384-well plates. siRNAs were diluted in Opti-MEM media (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to a concentration of 12.5 nM and mixed with 0.075 μL Lipofectamine RNAiMAX transfection reagent diluted in 9.925 μL Opti-MEM media (both reagents Thermo Fisher Scientific). After an incubation period of 20 min at room temperature to enable the formation of siRNA-transfection reagent complexes, HTBE cells were seeded on top (reverse transfection) and incubated for 36 h at 37°C, 5% CO
2
. Cells were then mock-treated or infected with influenza A virus strain A/WSN/1933 H1N1 at an MOI = 1, and cells were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO
2
. At 24 h post-infection, cells were fixed with 4% PFA (Boston BioProducts) for 30 min at room temperature and then washed twice with PBS. Cells were permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 for 20 min, followed by blocking with 3% BSA (Sigma) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary anti-IAV NP mouse monoclonal antibody HT103 (Mount Sinai, in-house) was added at 1:1000 dilution in BSA for 2 h at room temperature, followed by three washes with PBS and a 1-h incubation with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated anti-mouse secondary antibody (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# A-11001) diluted at 1:1000 in 3% BSA. Following three washes with PBS, cells were stained with DAPI (4,6-diamidine-2-phenylindole, KPL), and plates were sealed and stored at 4°C until imaging. Influenza A virus replication was assessed using high-throughput microscopy. Cells were imaged and analyzed using the Celigo Imaging Cytometer (Nexcelom Bioscience) to calculate the % of influenza A virus NP + cells (number Alexa 488+ objects/number DAPI+ objects).
PPMOs
PPMOs were synthesized by covalently conjugating the peptide (RXR)
4

Method details
Infections
California/4/09 (H1N1); Vietnam/1203/04 (H5N1-HALo) strains of IAV were generated at Mt. Sinai School of Medicine. Six to eight week-old female C57BL/6 mice (Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME) were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of a mixture of ketamine and xylazine (100 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg, respectively), and then 50 μL of infectious virus diluted in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) was inoculated intranasally (i.n.). To determine virus pathogenicity, five animals per group were infected i.n. with dose (1 × 10
4
PFU) and were monitored daily for weight loss for up to 14 days post infection (p.i.). Mice showing more than 25% of body weight loss were considered to have reached predefined humane endpoints and were euthanized. To determine viral pulmonary replication kinetics and to examine for genomics, proteomics and metabolomics, groups of 15 mice were inoculated with the indicated viruses (1 × 10
4
PFU per mouse). Mice inoculated with PBS served as controls. At 12h, 1, 2, 3 and 4 days p.i., 3 mice per experimental group were euthanized. Control animals were euthanized at 12h and 4 days post inoculation. The control animals sacrificed at 12h served as a control for IAV-infected animals at 12h, 1, and 2 days p.i. and the control animals sacrificed at 4 days p.i. served as the control for IAV-infected animals at day 3 and 4, respectively. For determination of viral titers, lungs were homogenized in 1 mL of PBS and viral titers determined by plaque assays with MDCK cells. To examine genomics, proteomics and metabolomics, lungs were homogenized in liquid nitrogen and divided in three equal amounts; also, homogenized lung samples were weighted, recorded, and shipped for analysis to genomics, proteomics and metabolomics cores. All animal studies were performed according to institutional guidelines and approved by the institutional care and use committee at Mt. Sinai School of Medicine.

Network propagation analysis
Network propagation was performed for all datasets—transcriptomics, abundance proteomics (AB), phosphoproteomics (PH) and ubiquitination proteomics (UB)—separately on the background of a STRING network using all edges with a score >600 (60% confidence). This STRING network comprises 18,966 genes connected by 976,668 edges. The maximum -log10(
p
) value per gene across time points and, in the case of UB and PH data, all sites, was used as starting “heat” to propagate. Propagation per omics type without mixing of different types of starting heat was performed by random walk with restart, with a restart probability of 0.2. The final score significance of propagated heat was determined by permutation analysis, permuting the starting heat among observed-genes-per-omics; 20,000 permutations. For permutation analysis, “self-heat” is subtracted from propagated heat, so that we only consider the heat propagated from other nodes on the network. “Self-heat” is defined as the portion of propagated-heat at each node that is the result of starting heat at that node. Additionally, the same network propagation was performed on the UB and PH datasets adjusted by AB. Finally, filtered RNA-seq data by adj.p.value <0.01 and abs(log2FC) > 2 was combined with the previous datasets, requiring
p
< 0.002 based on permutation analysis for all network propagation scores, resulting in a set of 2,920 significant genes.
Some RNA-seq genes could not be mapped to STRING identifiers, resulting in a set of 2463 genes for subsequent clustering. Clustering was performed using Diffusion State Distance (DSD)
97
to measure gene distances on a further subset of the STRING network that included only edges between the 2463 genes. DSD evaluates inter-gene distance based on similar results of random walks from the two genes, and was a major portion of the best overall method for network module detection in Choobdar et al
.

The DSD distance matrix was clustered using the partition around medoids procedure implemented in the
pam
function in the
cluster
package of R. Setting k to 24 modules (clusters) was chosen based on a local maximum in clustering score (average silhouette width), as measured by the
pamk
function in the
fpc
package, and visual inspection of the clustered distance matrix (see
Figure S2
).

Metabolomics
Polar and nonpolar metabolites were extracted from lung sample sets using a modified protocol developed by Bligh and Dyer.
100
Briefly, tissue was harvested in 100 μL methanol and lysed by three rounds of vortex (30 s), sonication, and snap freezing in liquid nitrogen (1 min/thaw). Polar and nonpolar metabolites were separated by partitioning after the addition of 750 μL 2:1 methanol:chloroform, 250 μL chloroform, and 250 μL water followed by vortex. Samples were stored at −20°C for 1 h and then centrifuged for 10 min at 10K rcf. The organic and aqueous phases were separated, and vacuum concentrated to dryness. Dried samples were stored at −80°C until analysis. Aqueous phase samples were reconstituted in 50 μL of 35% (v/v) acetonitrile in water and 5 μL of the sample was injected into the instrument for analysis. Polar metabolites were separated on a Micro200 LC (Eksigent) by hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC; Luna 3um NH2, 150 × 1 mm, 100 Å, Phenomenex). Mobile phase A consisted of water and 5 mM ammonium acetate, pH adjusted to 7.4 with ammonium hydroxide. Mobile phase B consisted of acetonitrile with 5 mM ammonium acetate (pH 7.4). The chromatographic method followed a gradient elution at 30 μL/min with the following conditions: 0–0.5 min 98% B, 0.5–1 min 95% B, 1–5 min 80% B, 5–6 min 46% B, 6–13 min 14.7% B, 13–17 min 0% B, 17–17.1 min 100% B, 17–23 min 100% B. The column eluent was directly flowed into a TripleTOF 5600+ mass spectrometer (Sciex, Framingham, MA) and analyzed in positive mode under the following parameters: 15 psi nebulizer gas, 20 psi heater gas, ion spray voltage 5000 eV, declustering potential 100 eV, TOF MS scan 60–1000 Da, fragmentation collision spread 25–40 eV. Data was acquired by Information Dependent Acquisition (IDA).
Metabolomics data processing and MidTOD development
Mass spectrometry data was aligned by retention time on Markerview software (Sciex, v. 1.2.1). Spectral peaks were aligned using the following parameters: 0.01 min minimum retention time, 0.50 min retention time tolerance, 0.05 Da mass tolerance, 0.01 Da minimum spectral peak width, 2 scan minimum retention time peak width, 8000 maximum number of peaks, peaks removed if found in less than 3 samples and area integrated from raw data. The resulting aligned peak lists were subjected to statistical analysis using artMS (Bioconductor), which formats metabolomics input files to be compatible with MSstats, an R-based statistical analysis software originally designed for proteomics data analysis. This pipeline analyzes spectral peaks, or features, identified by m/z and retention time, and evaluates the differences in peak intensities between treated and control samples. Default artMS settings were used, and the results are reported as pairwise differences in means between conditions as log2FC with a
p
value based on a two-sided t-test assuming equal variance across all conditions.
p
values were adjusted using the false discovery rate (FDR) estimated by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. A log2FC range of (±) 1.0 and FDR of 0.05 were selected for cutoff parameters. Metabolites were identified from the filtered peak list by Metabolite Identification Through Orthologous Datasets (MidTOD;
https://github.com/kroganlab/MIDTOD
). This custom R-based software was designed to integrate the metabolomics spectral data with data from related genomics and proteomics experiments. Metabolites are putatively identified by automated searching of the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database and the Human Metabolome Database (
https://hmdb.ca/
)
101
by molecular weight with a mass threshold of (±) 0.05 Da and a maximum molecular weight of 500 Da. Database hits are then restricted to metabolites that are matched to biologically linked proteins and genes found to be dysregulated by flu infection by the genomics and proteomics cores of the FluOMICs project (i.e., transcriptomics and proteomics analysis (see above and
Table S1

The MidTOD output consists of a list of putative identifications linked to significantly altered genes and proteins that are validated by matching MS/MS patterns and retention times to authentic standards. Common adducts (H+, NH4+, Na+, K+) are accounted for in the mass search.
MidTOD performance was tested using a decoy dataset containing metabolites identified with level 1 confidence to assess the accuracy of identification versus manual searching of the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB). Each m/z value was analyzed in MidTOD in both positive and negative mode for the +H or –H adduct, respectively. Results were matched to decoy dataset inputs to assess 1) if the correct identification was pulled and 2) the total number of putative identifications each feature was matched to. Features from the decoy dataset were input into HMDB mass search under the same parameters as MidTOD (positive and negative mode, H adduct only). HMDB results were assessed by determining if the correct identification was pulled and how many total possible identifications were assigned. Percentage of the correct identifications over the total possible identifications per feature was graphed using Graphpad Prism. Benchmarking was performed by comparing the overlap of metabolite and pathway identifications to Mummichog 3 (
https://mum3-prod.jax.org/#/analysis/new-analysis

Samples were briefly frozen in liquid nitrogen, thawed, and sonicated on ice three times. 1 mL of 1:1 MeOH:CHCl3 and 250ul HPLC grade water were added to each sample, and samples were vortexed and stored at −20°C overnight. Samples were centrifuged 10 min at 4°C, 7500 rpm to create a 3 layer suspension. The aqueous layer was removed via pipet and transferred to a new tube, and the organic layer was discarded. Extracts were dried in speedvac and stored at −80°C until analysis. Samples were resuspended in 1:1 ACN:H2O and analyzed with BEH Amide column (Waters) ABSciex 5600+ mass spectrometer. Proteinaceous phase was used for normalization across samples according to total protein amount. Targeted analysis was performed for four metabolites (arginine, glycine, GAA, and creatine) matched to m/z, RT, and MS/MS of authentic standards. Relative intensities were compared between treatment groups for each metabolite. Arginine (175.1 m/z) and glycine (76.0 m/z) were analyzed in negative mode. Creatine (132.0 m/z) and guanidinoacetate (118.0 m/z) were analyzed in positive mode.

HTBE siRNA experiments
To evaluate the effect of GATM knockdown in IAV replication, HTBE cells were transfected with siRNAs targeting GATM (Dharmacon siGENOME M-008900-01) or IAV NP (Dharmacon, custom sequence 5′ GGA UCU UAU UUC UUC GGA GUU 3′), or a negative control non-targeting siRNA (Dharmacon, custom sequence 5′-AAT CGA TCA TAG GAC GAA CGC-3′). Transfections were carried out in 384-well plates. siRNAs were diluted in Opti-MEM media (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to a concentration of 12.5 nM and mixed with 0.075 μL Lipofectamine RNAiMAX transfection reagent diluted in 9.925 μL Opti-MEM media (both reagents Thermo Fisher Scientific). After an incubation period of 20 min at room temperature to enable the formation of siRNA-transfection reagent complexes, HTBE cells were seeded on top (reverse transfection) and incubated for 36 h at 37°C, 5% CO
2
. Cells were then mock-treated or infected with influenza A virus strain A/WSN/1933 H1N1 at an MOI = 1, and cells were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO
2
. At 24 h post-infection, cells were fixed with 4% PFA (Boston BioProducts) for 30 min at room temperature and then washed twice with PBS. Cells were permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 for 20 min, followed by blocking with 3% BSA (Sigma) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary anti-IAV NP mouse monoclonal antibody HT103 (Mount Sinai, in-house) was added at 1:1000 dilution in BSA for 2 h at room temperature, followed by three washes with PBS and a 1-h incubation with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated anti-mouse secondary antibody (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# A-11001) diluted at 1:1000 in 3% BSA. Following three washes with PBS, cells were stained with DAPI (4,6-diamidine-2-phenylindole, KPL), and plates were sealed and stored at 4°C until imaging. Influenza A virus replication was assessed using high-throughput microscopy. Cells were imaged and analyzed using the Celigo Imaging Cytometer (Nexcelom Bioscience) to calculate the % of influenza A virus NP + cells (number Alexa 488+ objects/number DAPI+ objects).

Introduction
Influenza A virus (IAV) is a respiratory pathogen and member of the
Orthomyxoviridae
family that is responsible for significant morbidity and mortality. Several different strains with varying degrees of pathogenicity, virulence, and transmissibility circulate across the globe in a seasonal pattern and cause sporadic pandemics.
1
,
2
Each year, approximately 500,000 individuals worldwide die from IAV infection, and the threat of a pandemic similar to the 1918 outbreak remains high. Currently, treatment and prevention options include limited antivirals and seasonal vaccines that offer varying degrees of protection each year.
3
Disease mitigation measures are further hampered by the fact that IAV evolves rapidly, utilizing both antigenic drift through a high mutation rate and antigenic shift through the reassortment of genetic material between strains. This allows the virus to evade host immune responses, as well as IAV-directed antivirals and vaccines,
4
,
5
,
6
,
7
,
8
,
9
highlighting the need for new therapeutics and the identification of targets to facilitate drug development.
IAV contains a segmented, negative-sense, single-stranded genome that encodes up to twelve proteins involved in viral entry, genome replication, regulation of host immune responses, and virion release.
10
Additionally, the infection of cells requires the virus to co-opt host cell metabolism to obtain small molecule precursors,
11
,
12
,
13
rewire signaling,
14
and subvert organelle function.
15
The involved host factors represent an untapped pool for the development of host-directed therapeutics (HDT) against infection. Discovery of these potential host targets necessitates the use of tools that provide a comprehensive molecular view of infection, making IAV infection a prime subject for systems biology. Hence, several systems biology approaches have previously been applied to IAV infection, mostly focusing on one OMICs technology at a time. These have included large-scale functional genomic screens, as well as surveys of global changes to the transcriptome, and proteomic studies (e.g., König et al.
16
; Martin-Sancho et al.
17
; Li et al.
18
; Bogdanow et al.
19
; Yángüez et al.
20
; Weber et al.
21
). These studies have identified diverse potential host targets, such as CMK2B and GRK2, but have relied on cell line models of infection and on single data type readouts.
16
,
20
As a next step, the integration of complementary data types will be critical for understanding organ-specific changes that promote IAV pathogenesis;
22
however, due to the inherent challenges that data integration presents, research on this level is still rather sparse.
23
,
24
Here, we describe an integrative approach for complementary global OMICs analyses to examine infection in mouse lung with two strains of IAV. Using global transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic approaches to capture virus-induced changes in host factors over the course of infection, we provide a comprehensive picture of how IAV infection rewires lung physiology and alters inflammatory and immune parameters. To achieve the integration of the complementary datasets, we used network propagation analysis and developed a software called MidTOD –

atasets. These analyses reveal key nodes that are altered by IAV infection and identify a host dependency factor, GATM. Functional validation confirmed that reduced GATM expression was associated with decreased viral replication and dampened inflammatory responses during H1N1 infection
in vivo
.

A multi-OMICs dataset of influenza A virus infection in mouse lungs
IAV, like all viruses, must hijack cellular processes to sustain its replication, and these pathways represent a rich pool for therapeutic intervention as they are essential for viral pathogenesis but are less susceptible to the development of resistance. We sought to perform a comprehensive systems biology analysis of host factors important for sustaining infection in a mouse model of IAV infection. In order to capture the spectrum of virulence, disease severity, and transmissibility of IAV, we infected mice with two different strains, H1N1 A/California/04/2009 (referred to as H1N1), and H5N1 A/Vietnam/1203/04 (referred to as H5N1). The now seasonally circulating H1N1 strain emerged from the 2009 “swine flu” pandemic. It is a highly transmissible strain of swine origin that resulted in the infection of a large proportion of the world’s population within its first year of circulation, though it has a relatively low mortality rate. While human infections with the avian-origin H5N1 remain infrequent, it has led to smaller clusters of disease,
25
and is included as a potential pandemic strain of concern by the World Health Organization due to its mortality rate of >50%. In this study, we used a variant of this strain isolated from a fatal human case that was engineered to allow biosafety level 2+ work through a deletion in the HA polybasic cleavage site previously referred to as H5N1-HaLo.
26
Following the infection of C57BL/6 mice, lungs were isolated at 12, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h post infection and analyzed by transcriptomics, proteomics (abundance, phosphorylation, and ubiquitylation), and metabolomics (
Figure 1
A). To allow pathway mapping and interpretation of the sets of host factors that changed during infection, we subsequently performed the integration of this multi-OMICs dataset by using network propagation (see
Figure 2
), and the newly developed tool MidTOD (see
Figure 5
).

Network propagation identifies key pathway nodes involved in influenza A virus infection
While each of the collected data types offers insight into particular processes driven by IAV infection in mouse lungs, they individually provide an incomplete picture of host responses to viral infection. To increase the level of complexity covered in our network models, aiming to more fully describe the affected pathways during IAV infection, we set out to integrate the different data types, starting with transcriptomics and proteomics data. OMICs data integration is non-trivial, partially due to missing data per individual data type.
22
To overcome this challenge, we utilized a previously developed tool, network propagation, which allows for an expanded overlap between datasets by extending features measured for one data type onto a network of proximal genes or proteins.
27
,
28
For this, a signal in one data type will be spread to genes that are known to be associated with the gene of interest, analogous to heat diffusion through physically connected nodes. When signals from several datasets are included, this method allows the extraction of information on affected clusters of genes or pathways without requiring full overlap of datasets. To integrate transcriptomics and proteomics data collected over the time course of IAV infection, we thus developed a framework based on network propagation (
Figure 2
A and
STAR Methods
). Briefly, we performed network propagation on the background of a STRING network of mouse genes, revealing 2,920 genes that were changing significantly over the course of infection (
p
< 0.002;
Table S2
). Clustering these based on network proximity (
STAR Methods
) revealed 24 IAV-regulated functional modules (
Figure S2
), which we annotated based on Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis (word cloud annotations and associated genes shown in
Table S2
).
The clusters of genes we identified through this analysis are displayed in
Figure 2
B using a network model in which the size of each node represents the summarized significance of the genes in this module, and edge width represents the closeness of individual modules based on the underlying base network. Displaying multidimensional data is generally challenging, and network models such as the one we chose offer intuitive ways to convey dense information in 2D. We chose word clouds of enriched GO terms per module, and named each module with an overarching term representing important biological processes implicated by the genes in this cluster. Notably, the IAV-regulated functional clusters defined by our method showed varying contributions of the different data types, which is addressed by the colored node ring charts. For example, the cluster consisting of genes involved mainly in interferon signaling showed significant changes across the 4 different data types (
Figure 2
B, Cluster 3, all colored bars). Other clusters were driven by one data type over the others, such as the module consisting of genes associated with the actin cytoskeleton, which showed the majority of significant changes on the level of phosphorylation (
Figure 2
B, Cluster 11, green bars).
In summary, this integrated dataset of proteomics and transcriptomics data reveals functional modules affected during IAV infection that span across multiple cell biology processes. For example, our analysis confirmed an important role for innate immune response and interferon signaling: as highlighted by the large node size, network propagation notably culminated in Cluster 3, containing genes related to host response to viral infection and interferon signaling. Cellular structural rearrangements during influenza A virus infection
Not only does IAV infection lead to ISG induction and altered immune-related transcript abundance and protein function, it is also expected to impact other cellular signaling events on a global level. To test this, we employed an approach to predict changes in kinase activity. Using the Z-test enrichment method,
33

34

STAR Methods

This analysis predicted an upregulation of Casein Kinase II (CK2; driven by subunit CSNK2A1) during H5N1, but not H1N1 infection, and a strong down-regulation of LIM Domain Kinase 1 (LIMK1) activity for both virus strains. LIMK1, as well as the closely related Testis Associated Actin Remodeling Kinase 1 (TESK1) are both involved in actin signaling. This known pathway regulation is also reflected in our integrated network, where we found strong dysregulation of phosphorylation on a cluster of genes related to the actin cytoskeleton (

36

Rewiring of host metabolic processes by influenza A virus infection
Our network propagation analysis identified Clusters 7 and 17 that are associated with peroxisomal and mitochondrial metabolism. Previous work has supported the idea that host cell support of the IAV life cycle requires a virus-driven remodeling of energy metabolism,
40
nucleotide biosynthesis,
13
and lipid production.
12
We sought to better define these metabolic changes by integrating transcriptomic and proteomic changes with untargeted metabolomics in order to develop a comprehensive map of IAV-induced changes in lung metabolism. Untargeted metabolomics generates tens of thousands of signals, and the majority of these signals are not derived from the biological sample, but come from contaminants, adducts, and artifacts.
41
This results in a significant bottleneck in automating the identification of metabolites and complicates the integration of this data type with other OMICs analyses. Metabolite identification is performed by matching accurate mass and MS/MS patterns to data generated in-house through authentic standards to achieve level 1 identification or putative identification (levels 2 or 3)
42
if matched to metabolite databases. Additionally, tools such as genome restriction have been employed to characterize unknowns that are not currently in metabolite databases by incorporating information about compounds that could be potentially synthesized by an organism based on biosynthetic gene expression.
43
We hypothesized that, in addition to parameters such as MS/MS and retention time, utilizing information provided by changing genes or proteins in parallel OMICs datasets (e.g., RNA-seq or proteomics) to perform metabolite identification would increase both identification rates and throughput by connecting metabolites, proteins, and genes to pathways. Identified pathways can then be manipulated experimentally to confirm their function in regulating the physiological response to infection. To this end, we created the custom software MidTOD that 1) performs statistical analysis of untargeted metabolomic datasets and outputs the results in a format that allows the direct mapping of metabolites to gene and protein datasets, 2) restricts the identification to only significantly changing metabolites that are directly related to significant changes in transcriptomic and proteomic datasets, and 3) matches metabolites to gene and protein targets. In this way, the data output from the software can easily be used in modeling programs adapted to transcriptomic and proteomic analysis without reformatting, and reduces identification matches from metabolites such as xenobiotics that are not relevant to the system being studied, but are present in metabolomics databases. The level 2 or 3 identifications can also be matched to authentic standards to achieve level 1 identification (
Figures 5
A and
S5
A, and
STAR Methods
). We first tested MidTOD on a decoy dataset containing metabolites, which were validated by matching MS/MS and retention time with authentic standards under the same experimental conditions to achieve level 1 confidence (
Figure S5
B;
Table S5
). We compared the accuracy of identification for
m/z
values with a unique retention time in our decoy dataset by using either MidTOD or alternatively by performing a manual search in HMDB. MidTOD decreased the number of database hits for each feature and increased the accuracy of the identification compared to searching HMBD without the use of orthogonal datasets. Multiple database hits found using MidTOD were most often observed for isomeric compounds which cannot be resolved by mass. We subsequently benchmarked MidTOD against two other computational tools used to perform metabolite identifications and pathway mapping, MetaboAnalyst (Version 6.0)
44
and Mummichog (Version 3).
45
Our benchmarking was performed in two ways 1) we used the decoy dataset to identify the overlap in metabolite identifications between the three analysis tools and 2) we examined the number of endogenous and non-endogenous (xenobiotic) metabolites identified in our experimental datasets with each computational tool. MetaboAnalyst and Mummichog both showed high overlap with MidTOD in metabolites identified in the decoy dataset, indicating that overall, each tool is identifying similar metabolites (
Figure S5
C). MidTOD and MetaboAnalyst both identified similar percentages of endogenous and xenobiotic metabolites, while Mummichog identified fewer endogenous metabolites and an increased number of non-endogenous metabolites in our dataset (
Figure S5
D). Having benchmarked our tool, we then utilized MidTOD to perform a final integration step that incorporates the RNA-seq, abundance, ubiquitylation, and phosphorylation data obtained from the network integration with the untargeted metabolomic profiling. Overall, the highest number of metabolite IDs was obtained from at least two data types, with RNA-seq and UB datasets contributing to the highest number of ID matches (
Table S6
). Several enriched pathways were shared between H1N1 and H5N1 infection, and top hits included purine metabolism as well as related pathways such as the pentose pathway, responsible for the synthesis of NADPH and ribose (
Figure 5
B). Focusing on metabolites, genes, and proteins contained in Clusters 7 and 17 identified a network of amino acid catabolic processes (
Figure 5
C). Proteins involved in mitochondrial amino acid handling (enriched in Cluster 17) included the mitochondrial form of serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT2), a major regulator of nucleotide biosynthesis, and inducible nitric oxide synthase (NOS2), which is linked to citrulline and arginine metabolism (
Figure 5
D). Interestingly, inducible NOS2 is expressed by classically activated macrophages during infection and inflammation.
46
Additionally, a previous study showed that infection with the PR8 strain of influenza lead to increased levels of NOS2 in both macrophages and monocyte-derived macrophages and was associated with the development of lung pathology.
47
In Cluster 17, we also observed the sustained upregulation of GATM (Glycine Amidinotransferase), clustering with dysregulated metabolites (
Figure 5
D; see
Tables S1
and
S6
). GATM is a mitochondrial enzyme that functions as the rate limiting step in
de novo
synthesis of creatine,
48
a small molecule that is used to buffer ATP levels during cellular stress (
Figure 5
E). Taken together, the integration of our network propagation with metabolomics data via MidTOD highlights metabolic processes that could mediate host inflammatory or stress responses.

Glycine amidinotransferase is a host dependency factor for influenza A virus infection
We subsequently sought to determine a functional role during IAV infection for candidate genes identified in our network propagation analysis, including GATM. We first tested for host dependency and restriction factors using an RNAi screen in human lung cells (A549) that included both metabolic and non-metabolic host genes compiled from both the primary OMICs datasets and the integrated OMICs analysis (
Figure 6
A;
Table S7
). From this screen, we identified 17 host dependency factors, which included GATM, and 15 host restriction factors with a log2 fold-change greater than |2| (
Figure 6
B). Of note, the hit rate for this screen was slightly higher for the integrated dataset (14%) compared to candidates identified in the primary OMICs (9%). We then validated GATM as a potential host dependency factor in primary human tracheobronchial epithelial (HTBE) cells. Knockdown of GATM also significantly reduced the number of IAV-infected cells in these more physiologically relevant cells than the A549 cells, confirming a role for this protein in supporting IAV infection (
Figure 6
C).

In an effort to transiently reduce the expression of this enzyme specifically in the lungs of mice, we designed and synthesized peptide-conjugated phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomers (PPMOs) targeting GATM pre-mRNA or mRNA. PPMOs are antisense agents that are water soluble, enter cells readily, and are resistant to enzymatic degradation.

PPMOs can be delivered intranasally, increasing local concentrations in the lungs and eliminating potential side effects resulting from systemic administration.

in vivo

Discussion
In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of how IAV alters
in vivo
host gene expression, protein abundance, post-translational modifications (PTMs), and metabolism in mouse lungs. For this, we developed strategies to integrate and intuitively display complementary OMICs data collected over a time course of infection. This integrated systems biology approach allows us to interrogate host factors that reflect both viral hijacking of cell signaling and biochemical functions, and the host’s immune response to viral infection. Importantly, the datasets generated here are a rich resource for future studies analyzing host-pathogen interactions during respiratory infection.
Biological changes following influenza A virus infection in mice
Our network analyses identified several known and previously unknown perturbations associated with IAV infection. The largest module of the integrated network is related to IFN signaling and response to viruses, driven by relationships from transcriptomics as well as abundance and post-translational modification (PTM) data. This set of genes captures well-described pathways activated upon IAV infection, involving the mobilization of the host immune response
54
,
55
and cytokine signaling.
56
,
57
,
58
Further analysis of immune genes contributing to this node showed that both H1N1 and H5N1 IAV strains strongly induced transcriptional changes over the course of infection, even though H5N1 showed an earlier peak in pulmonary titers compared to H1N1. Of note, one cluster of transcripts that included both IFN-β and IL-6 was more strongly induced by H1N1 infection, with peak levels remaining lower after H5N1 infection. This correlates with the delayed kinetics of H1N1 viral replication we observe in pulmonary titers. Importantly, it is in line with previous reports that described the stronger repression of the interferon response in human cells by avian influenza strains.
29
,
59
,
60
Interestingly, we find that the ubiquitination of Stat1 on two sites (K525 and K592) follows that same trend (
Figure S3
C). The addition of ubiquitin is often a signal for proteasomal degradation, and has been described as a mechanism for the deactivation of STAT1 activity.
61
,
62
,
63
Additionally, many viruses are known to ubiquitinate host proteins to evade detection by the innate immune response (e.g., Garcin et al.
64
; Lin et al.
65
). However, we do not observe a decrease in protein abundance of Stat1 over the course of infection with either virus strain. This suggests a different function for the ubiquitination signal in this case. In fact, an increase in STAT1 transcriptional activity has been described upon ubiquitination by NKLAM.
66
Modules associated with the cytoskeleton –Clusters 11 (actin), 14, and 24 (cilia)– are also identified in our dataset. Rewiring of the actin cytoskeleton, although driven by multiple data types, was highly enriched for phosphorylation data. In line with this, the predicted downregulation of LIMK1, the kinase that phosphorylates Cfl1/2, leading to increased actin turnover and reorganization of actin filaments,
35
,
36
might point to the increased motility of certain subsets of cells. For example, immune invasion into the lungs could be one of the drivers of this phenotype, as the datasets we are looking at include a heterogeneous pool of cells, resulting from the homogenization of lungs prior to data collection. Furthermore, LIMK1 has been described to play a role in pulmonary endothelial cell-mediated responses to inflammation.
67
,
68
Pulmonary pathology during H5N1 infection is also captured by the depletion of transcripts associated with ciliated cells. CIBERSORTx subsequently identified loss of these cells by two days post-infection, and suggests that aberrant inflammation coupled to tissue loss may be one factor contributing to the pathogenesis of avian influenza viruses.
Linking metabolite data to the network propagation analysis highlighted the role of mitochondrial and peroxisomal metabolism in sustaining IAV infection, as shown by Clusters 7 and 17. GATM has previously not been characterized to play a role in IAV infection, and our study identified this protein as a host dependency factor. Previous work had highlighted a role for GATM in the development of colitis, and in GATM deficient mice, epithelial cells had higher levels of ATP deficiency and increased cell death.
69
In our study, we observed a trend toward decreased pulmonary titers in H1N1-infected mice after intranasal treatment with GATM PPMO, similar to what was observed with GATM siRNA
in vitro
. Additionally, and consistent with a role for the modulation of creatine levels during inflammation by GATM,
70
mice treated with GATM PPMO also show transcriptional alterations associated with IL-1β production and cell killing, pathways associated with the
in vivo
response to severe IAV infection.
71
This suggests that the downregulation of GATM could reduce IAV-associated pathology by both restraining viral infection and modulating the innate inflammatory response to reduce disease severity.
72
The GATM substrate, arginine, also serves as a precursor for NO synthesis. Indeed, our mapping of genes and metabolites identified by MidTOD connects NOS2 and GATM through arginine. It is likely that alterations in GATM also impact NOS2 function, which could alter innate immune responses although this remains to be tested. Several studies have pointed to a role for creatine metabolism in myeloid cells. The pharmacological depletion of creatine from bone marrow derived macrophages inhibited pro-inflammatory cytokine production and resulted in reduced IL-1 secretion,
73
mirroring the transcriptional changes seen in the GATM PPMO-treated mice. Intracellular and extracellular creatine levels also play a role in macrophage differentiation. GATM is highly expressed by alveolar macrophages, where it plays a role in Th2 differentiation
74
However, creatine supplementation has diverse effects on macrophage function. Within tumors, the addition of creatine promotes ATP production and skewing of macrophages to a pro-inflammatory, M1 phenotype.
75
In contrast, the deletion of the creatine transporter, Slc6a8, enhanced M2 differentiation. This suggests that the roles of exogenous creatine versus
de novo
biosynthesis on macrophage function are dependent on disease and tissue state.
Integration of complementary datasets: Network propagation and metabolite identification through orthologous datasets
The integration of transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets is inherently complicated by the different formats, both of raw and processed data, as well as the specific gaps in coverage of each OMICs technology. Of the technologies used in this study, transcriptomics provides the most complete coverage and is closely aligned with protein abundance measurements. As expected, the PTM measurements (phosphoproteomics and ubiquitination analysis) present complementary pictures of the proteome with a smaller overlap. This is attributable in part to gaps in coverage based on enrichment strategies and how well individual peptides are detected in MS analysis, but also reflects the fact that subsets of proteins will harbor either of these PTMs. These factors prevent the simple and straight-forward integration of multiple orthogonal datasets, despite the promise of a more comprehensive picture of the processes at hand.
22
To compensate for the expected incomplete overlap between data types and difficulty of data integration, we used two strategies: we developed a tool, MidTOD, for the mapping of metabolomics data to other OMICs data types, and used network propagation analysis to enrich pathways that are highly perturbed by infection. Network propagation aggregates signals from neighboring proteins in a pre-existing base network and thus magnifies biological phenomena through iterative connections between related genes or proteins.
28
This strategy has previously been used successfully to integrate orthogonal datasets, especially in the field of cancer systems biology (e.g., Leiserson et al.
27
; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al.
76
; Ruffalo et al.
77
), and has been applied to infectious disease studies (e.g., Eckhardt et al.
78
; Bouhaddou et al.
79
; Rathore et al.
80
).
While network propagation constructs related networks within the framework of known gene or protein interactions, metabolites lack a one-to-one correlation to individual proteins and/or genes, which prevents the incorporation of metabolite pool sizes into standard modeling programs. The regulation of metabolism occurs at both the enzyme and pathway level, and changes in the relative concentrations of metabolites do not provide information on the rate of particular reactions, or flux of metabolic pathways.
81
,
82
Linking changes in metabolite levels to alterations in protein abundance or post-translational modifications for regulated enzymes may add information on overall pathway activity. There are several software tools that perform metabolomic pathway analysis and employ different strategies to deal with identifying unknown features.
43
,
83
,
84
In this study, we had the advantage of collecting parallel proteomic and genomic information on the same sample sets to increase the throughput of metabolomic data analysis. Metabolite identification represents a significant bottleneck in data processing.
85
,
86
Here, we developed MidTOD, which uses the complementary proteomic (both abundance and post-translational modifications) and transcriptomic data to automate putative metabolite identifications and match them to genes and proteins. Identifying metabolites based on their relation to significantly changing genes and/or enzymes effectively reduces spurious hits to molecules of similar
m/z
that are present in current metabolite databases, but would not be related to the biology of the system. While software for restricting potential metabolite identifications to metabolites predicted to exist from the genome of the organism can be helpful,
43
a major advantage of MidTOD is that it also captures this information along with relationships among genes and proteins that are significantly altered by a process such as infection. It is important to note that imposing a
p
-value threshold for the orthogonal OMICs may limit identifications for metabolites that are not regulated by a particular disease process. However, critically, it identifies metabolites and pathways that participate in biosynthesis and signaling that can be functionally screened in additional high throughput assays.
In summary, we show that an integrative, systems biology analysis is a powerful tool to identify host factors involved in IAV infection. We note that these datasets can be mined for additional targets that modulate host responses to infection.
Limitations of the study
This study utilized C57BL/6 and BALB/cJ mouse models of IAV infection to investigate host immune responses. These two strains are commonly used to model IAV pathogenesis
87
,
88
and to test the efficacy of antiviral therapies and vaccines.
89
,
90
C57BL/6 mice were selected for the OMICs analyses, while PPMOs were tested in BALB/cJ mice. Although innate immune responses and cytokine profiles
91
differ between these strains, IAV-induced changes in GATM appear to be conserved. Further investigation of the factors identified in the OMICs screen is needed in additional infection models, such as ferrets, to better understand their broader relevance in host-pathogen interactions.
Our OMICs integration analysis identified the mitochondrial enzyme GATM as a key modulator of IAV pathology. The knockdown of GATM disrupted creatine biosynthesis, leading to a decrease in cytokine production and a reduction in disease pathology during infection. However, the specific cell types responsible for mediating these effects remain unidentified. Moreover, as GATM is the rate-limiting enzyme in creatine biosynthesis and plays a crucial role in regulating ATP levels, its disruption may impact mitochondrial function through mechanisms that have yet to be fully explored. Further investigation is needed to confirm the role of GATM and related pathways in other animal models of IAV infection, as well as in human subjects, to assess its potential as a therapeutic target.

Method details
Infections
California/4/09 (H1N1); Vietnam/1203/04 (H5N1-HALo) strains of IAV were generated at Mt. Sinai School of Medicine. Six to eight week-old female C57BL/6 mice (Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME) were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of a mixture of ketamine and xylazine (100 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg, respectively), and then 50 μL of infectious virus diluted in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) was inoculated intranasally (i.n.). To determine virus pathogenicity, five animals per group were infected i.n. with dose (1 × 10
4
PFU) and were monitored daily for weight loss for up to 14 days post infection (p.i.). Mice showing more than 25% of body weight loss were considered to have reached predefined humane endpoints and were euthanized. To determine viral pulmonary replication kinetics and to examine for genomics, proteomics and metabolomics, groups of 15 mice were inoculated with the indicated viruses (1 × 10
4
PFU per mouse). Mice inoculated with PBS served as controls. At 12h, 1, 2, 3 and 4 days p.i., 3 mice per experimental group were euthanized. Control animals were euthanized at 12h and 4 days post inoculation. The control animals sacrificed at 12h served as a control for IAV-infected animals at 12h, 1, and 2 days p.i. and the control animals sacrificed at 4 days p.i. served as the control for IAV-infected animals at day 3 and 4, respectively. For determination of viral titers, lungs were homogenized in 1 mL of PBS and viral titers determined by plaque assays with MDCK cells. To examine genomics, proteomics and metabolomics, lungs were homogenized in liquid nitrogen and divided in three equal amounts; also, homogenized lung samples were weighted, recorded, and shipped for analysis to genomics, proteomics and metabolomics cores. All animal studies were performed according to institutional guidelines and approved by the institutional care and use committee at Mt. Sinai School of Medicine.
Transcriptomics
To begin RNA extraction, mouse lungs were homogenized in liquid nitrogen. 1 mL Trizol was added per 50–100 mg of tissue and the homogenate was incubated at room temperature for 5 min 200 μL chloroform were added per mL of Trizol, shaken vigorously for 15–30 s and incubated at room temperature for 15 min. Samples were centrifuged for 15 min at 4°C and 12,000 rcf. The aqueous phase was carefully collected in a separate tube. 500 μL isopropanol was added per 1 mL Trizol, inverted to mix and incubated at room temperature for 5–10 min. Samples were transferred to Qiagen RNeasy Spin Columns and RNA was isolated according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA-seq libraries were constructed using the Illumina TruSeq Stranded Total RNA Library Prep Kit and samples were sequenced with an Illumina HiSeq 2500.
Sequencing reads were aligned to the California/4/09 (H1N1), Vietnam/1203/04 (H5N1-HALo), or mouse mm10 genome assembly using STAR,
92
which also produced segment- or gene-wise read counts. Differential gene expression analysis was carried out using DESeq2,
93
producing maximum likelihood log2 fold change (FC) values and Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted
p
-values via the Wald test. Heatmaps were drawn using non-blinded regularized log values from DESeq2.
Preparation of samples for global ubiquitination, phosphorylation, and protein abundance analysis
Frozen mouse lung tissue was homogenized in liquid nitrogen to a powder, resuspended in 8 M urea, 50 mM NH
4
HCO
3
, 150 mM NaCl, and PhosStop and Complete-EDTA free phosphatase and protease inhibitors (Roche), sonicated 3 times for 1 s at 30% power, and debris pelleted by centrifugation. Lysates were reduced by the addition of 4 mM TCEP (Sigma) for 30 min at room temperature, disulfide bonds were alkylated with 10 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma) for 30 min in the dark at room temperature, and excess iodoacetamide was quenched with 20 mM DTT (Sigma). Lysates were diluted 1:4 in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and trypsin (Promega) was added at a 1:100 enzyme:substrate ratio. Lysates were digested for 18 h at room temperature with rotation. Digested lysates were acidified to 0.1% TFA and peptides concentrated on Sep-Pak C18 solid phase extraction columns (Waters).
For protein abundance analysis, an amount of digested lysate equivalent to 100 μg of protein from each sample was labeled with TMT6-plex reagent according to the manufacturer’s instructions then combined. Trypsin (KR|P) was selected to allow up to two missed cleavages. Variable modifications were assigned for: N-terminal protein acetylation, and methionine oxidation. One static modification was assigned for carbamidomethyl cysteine. LFQ was enabled. Match between runs disabled. All other MaxQuant settings were left at the default.
The R packages MSstatsTMT and MSstats were used for quantitative analysis of abundance and PTM proteomics, respectively. For PTM, both phosphorylation (PH) and ubiquitylation (UB), the peptide ion intensities were summarized to a single intensity per unique observed single-peptide combination of modified sites (either PH or UB) by relabeling the protein of each feature as the combination of protein name and observed modified sites. From these models, these functions report pairwise differences in means between conditions as log2FC with a

Network propagation analysis
Network propagation was performed for all datasets—transcriptomics, abundance proteomics (AB), phosphoproteomics (PH) and ubiquitination proteomics (UB)—separately on the background of a STRING network using all edges with a score >600 (60% confidence). This STRING network comprises 18,966 genes connected by 976,668 edges. The maximum -log10(
p
) value per gene across time points and, in the case of UB and PH data, all sites, was used as starting “heat” to propagate. Propagation per omics type without mixing of different types of starting heat was performed by random walk with restart, with a restart probability of 0.2. The final score significance of propagated heat was determined by permutation analysis, permuting the starting heat among observed-genes-per-omics; 20,000 permutations. For permutation analysis, “self-heat” is subtracted from propagated heat, so that we only consider the heat propagated from other nodes on the network. “Self-heat” is defined as the portion of propagated-heat at each node that is the result of starting heat at that node. Additionally, the same network propagation was performed on the UB and PH datasets adjusted by AB. Finally, filtered RNA-seq data by adj.p.value <0.01 and abs(log2FC) > 2 was combined with the previous datasets, requiring
p
< 0.002 based on permutation analysis for all network propagation scores, resulting in a set of 2,920 significant genes.
Some RNA-seq genes could not be mapped to STRING identifiers, resulting in a set of 2463 genes for subsequent clustering. Clustering was performed using Diffusion State Distance (DSD)

DSD evaluates inter-gene distance based on similar results of random walks from the two genes, and was a major portion of the best overall method for network module detection in Choobdar et al
